steps.label: KP07 A loss turns “how wrong” into one number
A loss is one number · 1/8
steps.speakerNotes: The network gives an output; compared with the right answer, the loss function turns how far off into one number.

steps.label: A loss is one number · 1/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With this number we know which way to adjust the weights. This unit looks at regression, classification and hinge losses.

steps.label: A loss is one number · 1/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: with this number we know which way to adjust the weights regression measures distance; classification measures probability against the answer

steps.label: Shapes of regression losses · 2/8
steps.speakerNotes: MSE is the squared residual, a parabola, differentiable everywhere and very harsh for far points.

steps.label: Shapes of regression losses · 2/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: MAE is the absolute residual, a V, penalizing by distance only, robust to outliers but not differentiable at 0.

steps.label: Shapes of regression losses · 2/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Huber is quadratic near zero and linear far away, a compromise; delta must be tuned.

steps.label: Shapes of regression losses · 2/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Huber x: residual e · y: loss Huber quadratic for |e|\le\delta, else linear a compromise; tune \delta large residuals: MSE punishes hardest, MAE by distance, Huber is MSE near and MAE far

steps.label: The outlier's effect · 3/8
steps.speakerNotes: Residuals 1, 1, 1, 10; the last is an outlier.

steps.label: The outlier's effect · 3/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: MSE values 1, 1, 1, 100, total 103; the outlier is 97 percent.

steps.label: The outlier's effect · 3/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: MAE values 1, 1, 1, 10, total 13; the outlier is 77 percent.

steps.label: The outlier's effect · 3/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Huber's last value is delta times residual minus half delta, 9.5; total 11, 86 percent. This is what MSE being sensitive to outliers means concretely.

steps.label: The outlier's effect · 3/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: MSE nearly cares about that one point; MAE least; Huber is in between

steps.label: Cross-entropy · 4/8
steps.speakerNotes: Cross-entropy is minus the log of the probability given to the right class: the smaller the probability, the larger the loss, blowing up near 0.

steps.label: Cross-entropy · 4/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Reusing KP06's softmax output 0.665, 0.245, 0.090, mark them on the curve.

steps.label: Cross-entropy · 4/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: If the right class is the first, the loss is 0.408; the second 1.408; the third 2.408. Cross-entropy needs probability-like outputs, hence softmax or sigmoid in the output layer.

steps.label: Cross-entropy · 4/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: right class is 1 p=0.665,  -\ln p=0.408 right class is 2 p=0.245,  -\ln p=1.408 right class is 3 p=0.090,  -\ln p=2.408 the smaller the probability given to the right answer, the larger the loss; use softmax or sigmoid

steps.label: KL divergence · 5/8
steps.speakerNotes: Sometimes the target is itself a probability distribution, a soft label, as in distillation. Target 0.7, 0.2, 0.1 and prediction 0.665, 0.245, 0.090 are very similar.

steps.label: KL divergence · 5/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The KL divergence comes out at 0.0058, very close to 0.

steps.label: KL divergence · 5/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: If the target is one-hot, KL reduces to minus log 0.665, which is 0.408, the same as cross-entropy.

steps.label: KL divergence · 5/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: one-hot target (1,0,0) only \ln\frac{1}{0.665}=0.408 the same as cross-entropy similar distributions give a KL near 0; used with soft labels (e.g. distillation)

steps.label: Hinge loss · 6/8
steps.speakerNotes: Hinge is for binary classification with labels plus or minus 1; the loss is the larger of 0 and m minus y times f, here with m equal to 1.

steps.label: Hinge loss · 6/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Three points: y f equal to 1.5 gives loss 0; 0.3 gives 0.7; minus 0.5 gives 1.5.

steps.label: Hinge loss · 6/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The second point is classified right since 0.3 is above 0, yet it is within m of the boundary and still punished with 0.7. Unlike KP02's right-or-wrong 0-1 loss, this is continuous.

steps.label: Hinge loss · 6/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: right and far enough yf_o=1.5,  loss 0 right (0.3>0) but within m of the boundary yf_o=0.3,  loss 0.7 wrong yf_o=-0.5,  loss 1.5 unlike KP02's right-or-wrong 0-1 loss, hinge is continuous

steps.label: Two myths · 7/8
steps.speakerNotes: For the same residuals, MSE is 103 and MAE is 13.

steps.label: Two myths · 7/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: These two numbers have no meaning of one being larger; they are different rulers. Also, a smaller loss is not always better: it is measured on training data only and may just mean memorization.

steps.label: Two myths · 7/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: for the same residuals, 103 versus 13 does not mean one is larger They are different rulers. A loss is measured on training data only; a tiny loss may just mean memorizing it (KP04's generalization problem). a smaller loss is not always better; values of different losses cannot be compared

steps.label: Summary and preview · 8/8
steps.speakerNotes: Regression uses MSE, MAE, Huber; classification uses cross-entropy with a softmax or sigmoid output, KL for soft labels; margin classification uses hinge.

steps.label: Summary and preview · 8/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The Perceptron's loss only counts errors and is discrete; a continuous squared error lets us walk downhill step by step. That is ADALINE.

steps.label: Summary and preview · 8/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The Perceptron's loss only counts errors, so it is discrete and cannot be learned by gradients. With a continuous squared error we can walk downhill step by step. That idea is ADALINE. next unit: ADALINE and logistic regression
